title: A framework for the design interview
summary: A repeatable order for a system design interview: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch the API and data model, draw the high-level design, then deep-dive and address bottlenecks.
note:
1. Clarify: functional + non-functional (scale, latency, consistency) requirements
2. Estimate: QPS, read:write ratio, storage, bandwidth (back-of-envelope)
3. API + data model: a few endpoints, the core entities
4. High-level design: client → LB → services → cache/DB; draw the boxes
5. Deep dive: pick one component, discuss trade-offs
6. Bottlenecks: scale reads (cache/replicas), writes (sharding/queues), name SPOFs
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: What two kinds of requirements do you clarify first?
recall.a: Functional (what it does) and non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency).

recall.q: Why do a back-of-the-envelope estimate early?
recall.a: QPS, read:write ratio, and storage decide whether you need caching, replicas, or sharding, and justify later choices.

recall.q: After the high-level sketch, what are the last two steps?
recall.a: Deep-dive on one component with trade-offs, then identify and address bottlenecks and single points of failure.

shot.title: Interview order
shot.body:
| step | output | minutes (rough) |
|---|---|---|
| clarify | requirements list | 5 |
| estimate | QPS, storage | 5 |
| API + data | endpoints, schema | 5 |
| high-level | box diagram | 10 |
| deep dive | one component | 10 |
| wrap-up | bottlenecks, SPOFs | 5 |

sections.title: Clarify requirements
sections.body: ✍️ Pin down **functional** requirements (the features that must work) and **non-functional** ones (expected scale, latency targets, availability, consistency needs). Narrow scope explicitly — it is better to design two features well than ten vaguely.

sections.title: Estimate scale
sections.body:
✍️ Do a quick back-of-the-envelope: **QPS** (daily actions ÷ 86,400, times a peak factor), **read:write ratio**, **storage** (bytes/record × records × retention), and bandwidth. These numbers drive whether you need a cache, read replicas, or sharding.
```java
// e.g. 100M writes/day
double writeQps = 100_000_000.0 / 86_400;   // ~1,157/s
double peakQps  = writeQps * 3;              // headroom
```

sections.title: API and data model
sections.body: ✍️ List a handful of endpoints (`POST /tweet`, `GET /feed`) and the core entities and relationships. This grounds the design in concrete operations and exposes the main access patterns that decide SQL vs NoSQL and the shard key.

sections.title: High-level design
sections.body:
✍️ Draw the boxes and data flow: client → **load balancer** → stateless **services** → **cache** / **database**, plus a queue for async work.
- Keep it simple first, then justify each box from the requirements and estimates.

sections.title: Deep dive and bottlenecks
sections.body: ✍️ Pick one component (the feed generation, the counter, the dedup) and discuss its data structures and trade-offs in depth. Then name **bottlenecks** and **single points of failure**: scale reads with caching and replicas, scale writes with sharding or queues, and make the LB/DB redundant. Tie choices back to CAP/PACELC and the numbers you estimated.
